title: Lithium: levels, toxicity and interactions
blurb: Time and interpret lithium levels, follow the monitoring schedule, spot toxicity early and know what pushes levels up.
question: Brenda, 52, has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for 6 years. After two days of vomiting and diarrhoea she has a coarse tremor, slurred speech and is unsteady. What should the nurse do first?

teach.h: A drug with a narrow window
teach.body: NICE recommends lithium as the first-line long-term treatment for bipolar disorder. It has a narrow therapeutic index: the gap between an effective level and a toxic one is small. Lithium is cleared by the kidneys, so anything that reduces kidney clearance or body water raises the level. In plain English: lithium works well, but the level must be measured properly and protected from dehydration and interacting drugs.

items.label: after the last dose: take the level
mmol/L considered after relapse on lithium
Level 1 week after starting or any dose change

teach.caption: Stay at 3-monthly if aged 65 or over, on interacting drugs, at risk of renal or thyroid problems, poorly controlled, poor adherence, or last level 0.8 mmol/L or higher (CG185 1.10.19-1.10.20; BNF).

teach.body: Before starting: weight or BMI, U&Es including calcium, eGFR, thyroid function and full blood count, plus an ECG if there is cardiovascular risk. Every 6 months: weight or BMI, U&Es including calcium, eGFR and thyroid function. These pick up lithium's long-term effects on the kidneys, thyroid and parathyroid. People receive the lithium pack (booklet, alert card and record book), and lithium is prescribed by brand.

teach.caption: Neurotoxicity can occur even when the level is in the therapeutic range (CG185 1.10.24).

Examples

steps.sub: Coarse tremor, GI upset, confusion, ataxia

steps.sub: Do not give while awaiting advice

teach.h: Scenario: Brenda after a stomach bug
teach.body: In the community, Nurse Ahmed recognises that two days of vomiting and diarrhoea have dehydrated Brenda and likely raised her lithium. Coarse tremor, slurred speech and unsteadiness are toxicity signs. He advises her not to take the next dose, arranges same-day medical assessment with an urgent lithium level and U&Es, and asks about any new tablets such as ibuprofen. He documents and tells the prescriber.

teach.text: Fine tremor is a common side effect; coarse tremor suggests toxicity. And a 'normal' level does not rule toxicity out: if the person has neurological signs, treat it as toxicity. A level taken 2 hours after a dose reads falsely high, so always check the timing (12 hours post dose).

items: Lithium is first-line long-term treatment for bipolar disorder.
Levels 12 hours post dose; target 0.6–0.8 mmol/L when starting.
Levels weekly until stable, 3-monthly in year 1, then 6-monthly (3-monthly if higher risk).
Toxicity: coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion, ataxia; withhold and get urgent review.
Dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics raise levels; stop lithium over at least 4 weeks.

summary: You can now time and interpret lithium levels, follow the monitoring schedule and spot toxicity. You know which drugs and situations raise lithium and how it should be stopped.

A.q: When should a blood sample for a routine plasma lithium level be taken?
A.why: BNF: lithium levels are measured 12 hours after the dose, so results can be compared with the target range.

whyNot.0: A 6-hour sample is taken too early and reads higher than the standard.
whyNot.1: A 24-hour sample would read lower than the standard 12-hour level.
whyNot.2: A 2-hour sample is near the peak and would read falsely high.

A.q: Amira, 35, is starting lithium for the first time for bipolar disorder. What plasma level should usually be aimed for?
A.why: NICE CG185 1.10.15: aim for 0.6–0.8 mmol/L in people being prescribed lithium for the first time.

whyNot.0: This lower initial target is used for people aged 65 and over (BNF).
whyNot.2: This higher range may be considered after relapse on lithium, not at the start.
whyNot.3: This is above the recommended ranges and risks toxicity.

A.q: Which over-the-counter medicine should a person taking lithium be advised to avoid?
A.why: CG185 1.10.18: warn people about NSAIDs, including those bought over the counter, because they raise lithium levels.

whyNot.1: Paracetamol does not reduce lithium clearance and is the usual simple analgesic choice.
whyNot.2: Loratadine is not a recognised lithium interaction.
whyNot.3: Simple linctus is not a recognised lithium interaction.

B.q: Kwame, 47, stable on lithium, is started on bendroflumethiazide for hypertension. What is the main concern?
options: It may raise his lithium level
It may lower his lithium level
B.why: Thiazide diuretics reduce lithium excretion and raise levels; the prescriber should be alerted and levels checked more often (CG185 1.10.18; BNF).

whyNot.1: Thiazides increase, not decrease, lithium levels.
whyNot.2: Serotonin toxicity follows serotonergic drug combinations, not a thiazide.
whyNot.3: Agranulocytosis is the classic clozapine risk.

B.q: Peter, 40, has taken lithium for 3 years. He has no risk factors, takes no interacting drugs and his levels are stable at 0.7 mmol/L. How often should his level be checked?
B.why: CG185 1.10.20: after the first year, measure levels every 6 months, or every 3 months for people in higher-risk groups.

whyNot.0: Weekly levels are for the start and after dose changes until stable.
whyNot.1: Three-monthly applies in the first year or to higher-risk groups.
whyNot.3: Yearly is too infrequent for lithium levels.

B.q: Ruth, 58, on lithium, has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 2 days. She now has a coarse tremor and is unsteady on her feet. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give her dose with extra fluids and recheck tomorrow
Book a lithium level for her next routine review
Withhold lithium and arrange urgent level and review
Give loperamide and continue lithium as prescribed
B.why: Dehydration raises lithium. Coarse tremor and ataxia suggest toxicity: withhold the next dose and arrange an urgent level, U&Es and medical review (BNF; CG185 1.10.24).

whyNot.0: Giving more lithium while toxic worsens it.
whyNot.1: A routine booking delays treatment of possible toxicity.
whyNot.3: Treating the diarrhoea does not deal with the toxic lithium level.

C.q: Derek, 68, has taken lithium for 4 years with stable levels around 0.7 mmol/L and no interacting drugs. A student asks how often his levels should be checked. What is correct?
options: Every 6 months, as he is stable
Every 12 months, as he is long term
Every 3 months, because of his age
Every 4 weeks, because of his age
C.why: CG185 1.10.20 and BNF: continue 3-monthly levels for older people (BNF: 65 and over) even when stable.

whyNot.0: Six-monthly applies to stable adults without a risk factor; age 65 or over is one.
whyNot.1: Yearly is too infrequent for any lithium user.
whyNot.3: Four-weekly is more often than guidance requires for a stable person.

C.q: Ella, 44, has a lithium level of 0.7 mmol/L taken correctly at 12 hours. She is newly confused, has slurred speech and a coarse tremor. What should the nurse do?
options: Reassure her that the level is within range
Encourage fluids and repeat the level in 3 months
Give the evening dose and recheck the level tomorrow
Withhold lithium and seek urgent medical review
C.why: CG185 1.10.24: neurotoxicity can occur at therapeutic levels. Clinical signs of toxicity take priority over a normal number.

whyNot.0: A normal level does not rule out lithium neurotoxicity.
whyNot.1: Waiting 3 months ignores acute neurological signs.
whyNot.2: Giving more lithium while she has toxicity signs is unsafe.

C.q: Marcus, 50, has been well on lithium for 10 years and wants to stop. The team agrees. What advice is correct?
options: Reduce gradually over at least 4 weeks and watch for relapse
Stop it at once, as tapering is needed for antidepressants
Reduce over 1 week to limit the time on a lower dose
Stop it at once and start valproate the same day
C.why: CG185 1.10.25-1.10.26: reduce lithium gradually over at least 4 weeks, preferably up to 3 months, and monitor for mania and depression during and for 3 months after.

whyNot.1: Stopping abruptly raises relapse risk; tapering applies to lithium too.
whyNot.2: One week is shorter than the minimum 4-week taper.
whyNot.3: Abrupt stopping is unsafe, and valproate has strict MHRA restrictions.

reteach.title: Protect the narrow window
reteach.question: How do you keep a person on lithium safe?

blocks.body: Take the level 12 hours after the last dose. Keep the person hydrated and away from NSAIDs; flag new ACE inhibitors, ARBs or diuretics. Treat coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion or unsteadiness as possible toxicity, whatever the last level said.

blocks.text: Fine tremor: side effect. Coarse tremor: toxicity.

explain.body: Sample 12 hours after the last dose. Withhold the morning dose until the blood is taken. Check 1 week after starting and after each dose change, then weekly until stable.

test.q: A person takes lithium at 22:00. Their level is due tomorrow. When should the blood sample be taken?
options: At 10:00, an hour after the morning dose
test.why: 12 hours after a 22:00 dose is 10:00; the sample is taken before any further dose (BNF).

whyNot.0: 15 hours after the dose is outside the standard sampling time.
whyNot.1: A sample after a fresh dose reads falsely high.
whyNot.2: 20 hours after the dose would read lower than the standard.

explain.body: 0.6–0.8 mmol/L for people starting lithium. 0.8–1.0 mmol/L for at least 6 months may be considered after relapse on lithium or with subthreshold symptoms. BNF advises lower targets for people aged 65 and over.

test.q: Chen has relapsed while taking lithium at a level of 0.6 mmol/L. What range may the team consider for at least 6 months?
test.why: CG185 1.10.16: consider 0.8–1.0 mmol/L for at least 6 months after relapse on lithium.

whyNot.0: This lower range would reduce, not optimise, treatment after relapse.
whyNot.1: He relapsed within this range already.

explain.body: Every 6 months: weight or BMI, U&Es including calcium, eGFR and thyroid function. Lithium can impair the kidneys and cause hypothyroidism and hypercalcaemia.

test.q: Which blood test is part of the 6-monthly physical monitoring for lithium?
test.why: CG185 1.10.21: thyroid function is checked every 6 months with weight, U&Es including calcium, and eGFR.

whyNot.0: Prolactin is an antipsychotic monitoring test.
whyNot.2: Creatine kinase is not a routine lithium test.
whyNot.3: Clotting is not part of lithium monitoring.

explain.body: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers and diuretics raise lithium levels. So do vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, sweating, hot weather and low salt intake. Advise fluids and prompt help when unwell.

test.q: A person on lithium plans a beach holiday in a heatwave. What is the most important advice?
options: Take an extra dose on very hot days
Drink enough fluid and seek help if unwell
Avoid fluids with meals to protect the level
Switch to a low-salt diet while away
test.why: Sweating and dehydration raise lithium levels; adequate fluids and early help with vomiting or diarrhoea reduce toxicity risk (CG185 1.10.17).

whyNot.2: Restricting fluid causes dehydration and raises levels.
whyNot.3: Reduced salt intake raises lithium levels.
